chunks: "I think of it as two states per cycle. In the on-state, the high-side switch is closed, so the switch node is at V in .
The inductor now has V in-V out across it, so its current ramps up, and that current goes to the load and the output capacitor.
The inductor is storing energy in its magnetic field. In the off-state, the switch opens.
The inductor current can't change instantly, so the switch node swings down until the diode, or the low-side FET in a synchronous buck, takes over.
Now the inductor has -V out across it, so the current ramps down, still flowing into the load. The inductor is giving back its energy. The output capacitor smooths all that.
It supplies the load during the dips and absorbs the extra during the peaks. In steady state the current has to end each cycle where it started.
The up-ramp is (V in-V out)DT over L and the down-ramp is V out(1-D)T over L . Set them equal and you get V out equals D V in . The last piece is the feedback loop.
The controller compares a scaled copy of V out to a reference and nudges D up or down, so the output holds when the input or load changes."
